witnesses.provenance: Solana's per-transaction MAX_COMPUTE_UNIT_LIMIT is 1,400,000 compute units. It is the chain's limit, not ours. The campaign sets ProgramTest's ceiling to exactly that value and never raises it, so a transaction that did not fit would fail rather than be re-run with headroom. The direction matters: this is a chain limit the campaign must live under, not a measurement of ours restated as a target.

Solana's MAX_INSTRUCTION_STACK_DEPTH is 5, counting the top-level instruction as depth 1, so the deepest admissible `invoke [n]` line any program can produce is [5]. A complete Dealer transition runs Dealer -> Registry, Dealer -> Claims and Dealer -> Custody, and the Claims and Custody children invoke further; this witness is what would catch a composition change that put the family one hop from the runtime's hard stop.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.error != null) | select([.logs[] | select(contains("custom program error: 0x"))] | length == 0)] | length | tostring
witnesses.provenance: The Solana runtime reports a privilege, frame, or account refusal it decides ITSELF as a bare InstructionError with no `custom program error:` log line; that line appears only when a program returned ProgramError::Custom. TIERS.md draws exactly this distinction and records a pre-taxonomy refusal as an unnamed one, because crediting it would overstate what the program proved. Every transaction in this tier is a refusal, so this witness is the whole tier's admissibility: it asserts that not one of them was bounced by the runtime before the Dealer ELF ran.

A route is EXECUTED in this census only on a succeeding transaction. This tier deliberately builds no activated release set, no admitting Core Market phase, and no Claims/Custody prestate, so nothing in it may succeed. Pinning that to zero rather than leaving it unsaid means a future change that made one of these hostile cases pass would fail the tier instead of quietly flipping a census row on the strength of a weakened refusal, which is the failure mode AGENTS.md names: do not weaken a refusal to make an integration test pass.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.label | test("into the release waist")) | select([.logs[] | select(test("invoke \\[2\\]"))] | length > 0)] | length | tostring
witnesses.provenance: This INVERTS `the-release-cases-actually-invoked-the-registry`, which required an `invoke [2]` on every release case. That requirement stopped being true at `c202ee3d` ("families: read the activation cache the Registry owns, and stop calling it"), which retired the `RegistryInstructionV1::Reauthenticate` CPI. Both of its failure modes are worth recording because they are the two ways a stale witness hides: it would have FAILED once the campaign got that far, and it never got that far, because the test's own assertion on the same retired CPI panicked first and `set -e` aborted the run before any witness was evaluated; then, the moment the campaign's labels were corrected to say `release waist`, its `select` matched nothing, counted zero and reported OK while asserting nothing at all. A witness that keys on a label is green both when the property holds and when the label is gone. What is pinned now is the property that commit established and that a regression would break: Dealer is reached as a CHILD of a Registry continuation already at CPI depth one, so calling the Registry back is reentrancy that Solana refuses before Dealer can do any work (`programs/dclutch-dealer-sbf/src/lib.rs:1167-1175`). The waist must therefore be a read of the Registry-owned cache through the Registry's own crate, and any `invoke [2]` appearing on one of these transactions means the reentrant call came back.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.label | test("into the release waist"))] | length | tostring
witnesses.provenance: The non-vacuity guard for the two witnesses above it, and the reason this file gained a row rather than only edits. Both of those select on a label substring and then count violations, so both report OK when the substring matches NOTHING -- which is exactly how the retired-CPI witness stayed green through the change that invalidated it. Renaming the campaign's labels must fail loudly here instead of silently emptying the other queries. Eight is the release loop's own arm count in `programs/dclutch-dealer-sbf/program-test/tests/family.rs`, one per Dealer action.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.label | test("Liquidity into the release waist")) | .error] | sort | join("|")
witnesses.provenance: This replaces `both-liquidity-actions-are-unreachable-at-every-offered-slot`, which pinned a contradiction and was written to fail the day it was fixed. It was fixed: `Request::validate_shape` and `authenticate_clock` had each restated which actions carry a slot, and disagreed, so AddLiquidity and RemoveLiquidity needed `now == 0` to encode and `now == clock.slot` to authenticate and no slot the chain can offer satisfied both. `Action::now_discipline` in crates/dclutch-dealer-codec/src/lib.rs is now the single owner of that fact and both sides read it. What is pinned here is the OTHER direction, which is what a regression would break: the two liquidity actions get past instruction shape, the 23-account frame, identity, their actor rule and their Clock rule, and refuse at the release waist (`DealerSbfError::Release`, 0x7005, which `InstructionError` renders in decimal as 28677) like the other five actions. A reintroduced Clock disagreement shows up here as `Clock`, 0x7004 / 28676. The waist was a Registry CPI when this witness was written and is a Registry-owned cache read since `c202ee3d`; the code it refuses with is unchanged, which is why only the label regex moved.

witnesses.query: [.transactions[] | select(.label | test("carrying a slot in its padding")) | .error] | sort | join("|")
witnesses.provenance: The hostile half of the same rule. `DClutchSemantics.DealerLiquidity.Command` carries a slot only inside `Replacement`, `Activation` and `Fill`; `enterTerminal`, `unwind`, `retire`, `addLiquidity` and `removeLiquidity` have no time coordinate at all, so their `now` is padding and one semantic request must have exactly one encoding. The campaign patches a real slot straight into the wire bytes for RemoveLiquidity, EnterTerminal and Unwind -- the encoder will not produce that form -- and each must refuse at decode with Instruction (0x7000, rendered in decimal as 28672). Without this, relaxing the padding rule to 'fix' a clock complaint would admit 2^64 encodings of the same liquidity adjustment, each with its own request digest.
